newsitem.title: CHINA: China turns up heat on Taiwan after HK handover.
newsitem.headline: China turns up heat on Taiwan after HK handover.

text.p: China turned up the heat on Taiwan within hours of taking back Hong Kong, delivering a rousing call for reunification.
But Taipei cold-shouldered the communist giant, and said reunification was only possible under multi-party democracy.

China saw Britain's handover of Hong Kong putting an end to 156 years of national humiliation. Next on the agenda for a more prosperous and increasingly self-confident Beijing is Taiwan, which it regards as a renegade province.

"The prospect of complete national reunification... now stands promisingly in sight," Chinese President Jiang Zemin told a jubilant Beijing rally on Tuesday night that was topped by a thundering display of 2,000 fireworks.
Chinese leaders see Hong Kong -- returned to Beijing under a "one country, two systems" formula -- as a model for Taiwan.
But Taiwan's Vice-President Lien Chan said reunification could only be achieved democratically, dubbing his solution: "one country, one good system."
The Taiwan stock market on Wednesday shook off its uncertainty and signalled its approval for Hong Kong's return to the motherland after 165 years of British rule.
After being on holiday since the Monday midnight handover, the weighted index in Taipei was up 73.72 points, almost one percent, in the first half hour on brisk trading.
"The uncertainty of the handover is gone," said Lin Long-hsien, senior analyst for United Securities. "The market will now relax and continue with its recent bull run."
Hong Kong's stock market reopens on Thursday after closing last Friday for the handover.

Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate handpicked by Beijing to run Hong Kong, produced a policy blueprint for its 6.4 million people, pledging in his inaugural address to curb property speculators, boost land reclamation and improve education.
His ambitious goals for this thriving capitalist enclave won a mixed reception on Wednesday.

"This speech might have disappointed those Hong Kong people who had expected a major announcement from him... But it was discreet and reasonable for Tung Chee-hwa to focus on principles and avoid details," said the independent Chinese-language Apple Daily.
"Hong Kong people share Mr Tung's vision. It is in bringing the vision to reality that there are some doubts," said the English-language Hong Kong Standard.

About 10,000 pro-democracy activists mounted their own answer to Beijing's rule with a march in torrential rain through the heart of Hong Kong's financial district on the day that China took control of one of the world's richest economies.

Despite the presence in the region since dawn on Tuesday of 4,000 armour-supported troops of the People's Liberation Army, they vowed to continue to commemorate yearly the 1989 Tiananmen massacre which caused such trepidation in Hong Kong.
In Singapore, Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew was quoted on Wednesday as saying the freedom of the Western media in Hong Kong would not continue unabated.

The Straits Times daily said Lee had told Singapore reporters in Hong Kong on Tuesday that journalists from the West could not "use a part of China to keep on every day throwing poison darts at Chinese leaders."
"They've got to make up their minds, either they accept certain realities or they will face a very unfriendly government," he said.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Tuesday he had won assurances from Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen that the PLA would never take to the streets of Hong Kong in armoured cars, as they did at Tiananmen.
Hong Kong was coming quietly to the end of a five-day holiday to celebrate the handover, preparing for the Thursday reopening of its share market.
The market went on a rollercoaster ride in the leadup to the handover with "red chip" mainland company stocks soaring to new highs.
London currency analysts believe the Hong Kong dollar is likely to avoid a handover hangover and take the new regime in its stride.
"The foreign currency reserves of the Hong Kong authority are so massive, they would crush any sort of speculative attack on the currency," said one London currency analyst.

Hong Kong and Chinese officials are keen to maintain the currency's stability and stress the continuation of the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar and the independence of Hong Kong's monetary system from China.

Tung, seeing a string of visiting foreign ministers and handing out special awards to local dignitaries on Wednesday, is eager to maintain business confidence, calling Hong Kong "the freest and most vibrant economy in the world."
But communism and capitalism have never been happy bedfellows and international financiers will be riveted to see how the market's Hang Seng Index performs once the giant handover party is over.
